title: Physics
text:
Physics is the natural science that studies matter, its motion and behavior through space and time, along with related concepts such as energy and force, with the goal of understanding how the universe behaves at its most fundamental level.

Physicists seek to uncover the underlying laws and mechanisms governing natural phenomena across all scales, from subatomic particles to galaxies and the cosmos as a whole.

The field encompasses diverse branches, including classical physics areas such as mechanics (describing motion and forces in everyday and macroscopic systems), thermodynamics (addressing heat, energy transfer, and statistical behavior of systems), electromagnetism (governing electric and magnetic fields), and optics (studying light and its interactions); as well as modern physics branches like quantum physics (exploring matter and energy at atomic and subatomic scales), relativity (handling high speeds and strong gravity), nuclear physics (focusing on atomic nuclei and reactions), astrophysics (applying physics to stars, galaxies, and cosmic origins), and applied areas such as medical physics (using physics in diagnostics and treatments) and optics/photonics (advancing light-based technologies).

Through theoretical modeling, mathematical frameworks, and experimental research, physics provides principles that form the basis for fields such as chemistry, biology, and engineering, and supplies explanations of natural phenomena across disciplines.

#History of physics

#Ancient physics

The earliest systematic inquiries into the physical world emerged in ancient Mesopotamia and Greece, where observations of natural phenomena transitioned from mythological explanations to rational and naturalistic accounts.

Babylonian astronomers, active from the early 2nd millennium BCE, compiled extensive records of celestial movements, including planetary positions, lunar cycles, and eclipses, providing empirical data that later influenced Greek models. These observations enabled predictions of astronomical events and laid foundations for a geocentric understanding of the cosmos.

In ancient Greece, the pre-Socratic philosophers of the 6th and 5th centuries BCE initiated natural philosophy by seeking a fundamental principle (archē) to explain the origin and nature of the cosmos, rejecting purely divine causation in favor of inherent material processes. Thales of Miletus proposed water as the archē, viewing it as the source from which all things arise and to which they return, influenced by its role in nourishment and generation. Anaximander identified the archē as the apeiron (the boundless or indefinite), an eternal substance from which opposites like hot and cold separate to form the world in a regulated cycle. Anaximenes posited air as the archē, transforming into other substances through condensation (yielding water, earth) and rarefaction (yielding fire).

These early thinkers grappled with the problem of permanence amid apparent change. Heraclitus emphasized constant flux, describing the cosmos as an ever-living fire governed by logos (rational order) and the unity of opposites, where strife drives transformation. In contrast, Parmenides argued that true reality is unchanging, eternal, and singular "what-is," rendering perceived change and plurality illusory and accessible only through reason rather than senses. Empedocles reconciled these views by proposing four eternal "roots"—earth, water, air, and fire—as the fundamental building blocks of matter, mixed and separated cyclically by the forces of Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion), thus explaining change without true creation or destruction. The atomists Leucippus and Democritus later advanced a mechanistic view, positing indivisible atoms moving in a void, with all phenomena arising from atomic combinations differing in shape, arrangement, and position.

Aristotle (384–322 BCE) synthesized and systematized earlier ideas into a comprehensive natural philosophy, particularly in his Physics. He adopted the four elements—earth, water, air, and fire—each possessing inherent qualities of heaviness or lightness that determine natural motion toward their proper cosmic places: earth and water move downward toward the center, while air and fire move upward toward the periphery. Natural motion occurs spontaneously when obstacles are removed, aligning with an element's inherent tendency, whereas violent (forced) motion requires continuous external movers, as seen in projectile motion where displaced air sustains movement after the initial impulse. Aristotle defined motion broadly as the actuality of a potentiality, distinguishing it from rest and emphasizing teleological explanations through four causes: material, formal, efficient, and final. His framework integrated observation with philosophy, positing a cosmos divided into a changeable sublunary realm of the four elements and an eternal celestial realm of circular motion.

Ancient Greek astronomy built on Babylonian data to develop a geocentric model, placing Earth at the center of a spherical cosmos. By the 5th century BCE, observations such as Earth's round shadow during lunar eclipses supported a spherical Earth. Eudoxus introduced concentric crystalline spheres to account for planetary motions through uniform circular paths, a system Aristotle incorporated and expanded with aether as a fifth element for celestial perfection and eternal rotation. These qualitative models prioritized philosophical coherence over precise prediction, though they incorporated empirical evidence from earlier observations.

#Scientific Revolution

The Scientific Revolution in physics, spanning the 16th and 17th centuries, represented a fundamental shift from qualitative, Aristotelian descriptions of nature to quantitative, empirical, and mathematical approaches that form the basis of modern science. This transformation emphasized systematic observation, experimentation, and the application of mathematics to describe physical phenomena, replacing reliance on philosophical deduction with testable hypotheses and precise measurements.

Johannes Kepler, drawing on meticulous observational data collected by Tycho Brahe, formulated three laws of planetary motion that provided a mathematical framework for understanding orbits under the heliocentric model. His first law states that planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus; the second law indicates that a line connecting a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, implying varying orbital speeds; and the third law relates the square of a planet's orbital period to the cube of its average distance from the Sun. These laws, published between 1609 and 1619, marked a departure from assumed circular orbits and demonstrated the power of mathematical analysis applied to empirical data in describing celestial mechanics.

Galileo Galilei advanced the emerging experimental method through quantitative studies of motion on Earth, particularly using inclined planes to investigate falling bodies and inertia. By rolling balls down ramps and carefully measuring distances and times while minimizing friction, Galileo showed that objects accelerate uniformly under gravity and that, in the idealized absence of resistance, a moving object would continue indefinitely at constant speed—a concept foundational to inertia. These experiments, combined with his analysis of projectile motion, illustrated the interplay between mathematical theory and controlled experimentation, establishing a rigorous approach to uncovering natural laws.

The period also witnessed the birth of the modern experimental method as a core scientific practice, with natural philosophers increasingly conducting systematic tests under controlled conditions rather than relying on traditional authority or untested speculation. Early mathematical modeling of nature gained prominence, as seen in Galileo's insistence on the mathematical character of physical laws and Kepler's orbital calculations, setting the stage for unified descriptions of motion. These advancements in experimentation and quantification culminated in Isaac Newton's synthesis of terrestrial and celestial mechanics.

#19th century physics

The 19th century marked the maturation of classical physics through the unification of disparate phenomena and the emergence of new fields that provided a comprehensive framework for understanding heat, energy, and electromagnetism. Advances in experimental techniques and theoretical synthesis revealed that many seemingly unrelated effects shared common underlying principles, leading to the formulation of foundational laws that unified mechanics, heat, and electrical phenomena.

The principle of conservation of energy emerged as a central unifying concept during the 1840s. Julius Robert Mayer, a German physician, first articulated the idea in 1842, proposing that heat and mechanical work are equivalent and interconvertible forms of energy based on observations of blood color in different climates and comparisons of specific heats of gases. James Prescott Joule, working independently in England, provided rigorous experimental confirmation through the 1840s, notably using paddle-wheel experiments to measure the mechanical equivalent of heat by converting mechanical work directly into heat in insulated water. Hermann von Helmholtz further generalized the principle in 1847, extending it to all natural forces. Their combined efforts established that energy is neither created nor destroyed but merely transformed, replacing earlier notions of caloric substance.

Thermodynamics developed as a distinct discipline from the 1820s onward, building on these insights. Sadi Carnot's 1824 analysis of ideal heat engines emphasized the role of temperature differences in producing work from heat flow. Joule's experiments in the 1840s bridged mechanical and thermal processes by demonstrating heat production from work. By 1850, Rudolf Clausius and William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) formulated the first and second laws of thermodynamics: the first restating energy conservation in thermal contexts, and the second addressing the directional nature of heat flow. These laws formalized the interconversion of heat and work while accounting for irreversible processes in real engines.

The kinetic theory of gases provided a microscopic explanation for macroscopic thermal phenomena. In the 1850s, Clausius advanced the theory by recognizing heat as the kinetic energy of random molecular motion and introducing concepts like mean free path. James Clerk Maxwell built on this in the 1860s, developing a statistical treatment that described molecular velocity distributions and derived key gas properties from molecular collisions. This approach linked observable thermodynamic behavior to the motion of invisible particles.

The unification of electricity and magnetism progressed through experimental and theoretical work. In the 1820s and 1830s, André-Marie Ampère established electrodynamics by showing mechanical forces between currents, while Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, demonstrating that changing magnetic fields produce electric currents. Faraday also developed field concepts based on lines of force. James Clerk Maxwell synthesized these findings in the 1860s, creating a unified theory of electromagnetism that treated electricity and magnetism as interconnected aspects of a single field.

#20th century physics

The 20th century marked a profound transformation in physics through the emergence of relativity and quantum mechanics, which replaced classical descriptions and established the foundations of modern understanding of the universe at both macroscopic and microscopic scales.

In 1905, Albert Einstein introduced special relativity in his paper "On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies," reconciling mechanics with electromagnetism by asserting the constancy of the speed of light in vacuum for all inertial observers and the equivalence of physical laws across inertial frames. Einstein completed the general theory of relativity in November 1915, describing gravity geometrically as the curvature of spacetime induced by mass and energy, providing a framework that explained gravitational phenomena beyond Newtonian limits.

Quantum mechanics developed rapidly in the mid-1920s. Werner Heisenberg formulated matrix mechanics in 1925–1926, emphasizing observable quantities such as spectral line frequencies and intensities while avoiding classical trajectories. Independently, Erwin Schrödinger developed wave mechanics in 1926, representing quantum states through wave functions governed by his equation and interpreting atomic orbitals as standing waves. These mathematically equivalent formulations provided a complete theoretical framework for atomic-scale phenomena.

Quantum field theory originated in the late 1920s, with Paul Dirac's 1927 paper "The quantum theory of the emission and absorption of radiation" introducing the quantization of the electromagnetic field and describing photons as excitations, thereby establishing quantum electrodynamics as the first quantum field theory. Subsequent work by Dirac, Heisenberg, Pauli, and others in the late 1920s and early 1930s formalized canonical quantization of fields and extended the approach to relativistic electrons.

In cosmology, the Big Bang model began with Georges Lemaître's 1927 proposal of an expanding universe originating from a dense primeval state, later supported by Edwin Hubble's 1929 observations of systematic galactic redshifts indicating universal expansion. Efforts to unify quantum mechanics with general relativity have continued to shape theoretical physics frontiers.

#Fundamental concepts

#Matter and energy

Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space (has volume). In classical physics, this includes all substances with rest mass. Ordinary matter, such as everyday objects, is primarily composed of atoms, which consist of a central nucleus containing positively charged protons and neutral neutrons, surrounded by a cloud of negatively charged electrons. Elements are pure substances consisting of atoms with the same number of protons (atomic number), and they cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means. There are 118 known elements, with 94 occurring naturally (some in trace amounts).

Matter exists in four primary states—solid, liquid, gas, and plasma—depending on the arrangement, motion, and ionization of its particles. Solids have definite shape and volume, liquids have definite volume but take the shape of their container, gases have neither definite shape nor volume, and plasma consists of ionized gas with free electrons and ions that respond to electromagnetic fields (plasma is the most common state of ordinary matter in the universe, e.g., in stars).

Energy is the capacity to do work or transfer heat, existing in various forms that can convert from one to another. Energy is fundamentally classified as kinetic (energy of motion) or potential (stored energy). Kinetic energy includes the energy of moving objects, thermal energy (random motion of atoms and molecules, also called heat), radiant energy (electromagnetic waves such as light), electrical energy (flow of electrons), and sound energy (vibrational waves). Potential energy includes gravitational (due to position in a gravitational field), chemical (stored in atomic bonds), mechanical (stored by tension, such as in springs), and nuclear (stored in atomic nuclei).

In modern physics, matter and energy are interchangeable, as established by Albert Einstein's special relativity. The mass-energy equivalence is expressed by the equation E = mc², where E is energy, m is mass (rest mass), and c is the speed of light in vacuum. This relation shows that mass is a form of stored energy (rest energy), and a small amount of mass can convert into a large amount of energy, as observed in nuclear reactions.

#Space and time

Space and time form the fundamental arena in which physical events occur, providing the framework for describing position, motion, and duration in both classical and modern physics.

In classical physics, Isaac Newton articulated a substantival view of absolute space and absolute time in the Scholium to the definitions of his Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687). Absolute space is independent of external objects, remains always similar and immovable, and serves as the fixed background against which true motion is measured. Absolute time flows uniformly and equably, without relation to any external phenomena or motion. This framework distinguishes true motion, such as acceleration or rotation, as change relative to absolute space rather than merely relative to other bodies. Newton's famous bucket experiment illustrates this: the concavity of water in a spinning bucket demonstrates motion relative to absolute space, even when no relative motion exists between the water and the bucket.

Opposing Newton's substantivalism, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed a relational theory of space and time. Space is an order of coexistences among bodies—an ideal abstraction from relations of distance and situation—while time is an order of successions. Neither space nor time exists independently as a real entity; they arise from relations between material objects and are added by the mind. Leibniz argued that true motion is grounded in internal force (vis viva) rather than change relative to an absolute framework. In the 19th century, Ernst Mach extended relational critiques, proposing that inertial effects, such as resistance to acceleration, originate from relations to the distribution of distant matter in the universe rather than an absolute space. Mach's ideas challenged Newton's absolute framework by seeking to explain inertia through relations among bodies alone.

In classical mechanics, motion is described relative to reference frames—sets of points or objects at rest relative to one another, equipped with a time standard. An inertial reference frame is one in which Newton's laws of motion hold: a body subject to no forces moves with constant velocity in a straight line, accelerations are proportional to applied forces, and action-reaction pairs are equal and opposite. Frames moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame are also inertial, reflecting the principle of relativity in classical physics. Absolute space provided a preferred inertial frame in Newton's view, though empirically indistinguishable from other inertial frames due to the equivalence of uniform motion.

The early 20th century saw the introduction of spacetime as a unified four-dimensional continuum. Hermann Minkowski reformulated the description of physical events by combining three spatial dimensions with time into a single manifold, where space by itself and time by itself recede into mere shadows, and only their union retains independent reality. Physical phenomena are represented as worldlines tracing paths through this four-dimensional world, with laws of physics expressed as relations between these worldlines. In general relativity, spacetime is further curved by the presence of matter and energy.

#Force and motion

Force is a push or pull that acts on an object as a result of its interaction with another object. This interaction can change the object's motion by making it start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction. Forces are ubiquitous in everyday experience, such as when a person pushes a door open or pulls a rope, and they always arise from interactions between objects.

Motion describes a change in an object's position over time. It can be classified into uniform motion, where an object moves at constant velocity (constant speed in a straight line), and accelerated motion, where velocity changes (either in speed, direction, or both). For example, an object moving at a steady rate along a straight path exhibits uniform motion, while one speeding up or turning a corner undergoes accelerated motion.

Inertia is the natural resistance of an object to any change in its state of motion. An object at rest tends to remain at rest, and an object in motion tends to continue moving at constant velocity unless acted upon by an external force. Inertia is directly related to mass: the greater the mass, the greater the inertia and the more difficult it is to change the object's motion. This concept is formalized in Newton's first law of motion.

Force and velocity are vector quantities, meaning they have both magnitude and direction. Velocity describes the rate of change of position, incorporating both speed and direction, so two objects with the same speed but opposite directions have different velocities. Force similarly requires specification of magnitude (how strong) and direction (where it acts) to fully describe its effect on motion.

#Conservation laws

Conservation laws are fundamental principles in physics that state certain physical quantities remain unchanged over time within an isolated system, where no external influences act on the system. These laws arise from deep symmetries in the laws of nature and serve as powerful constraints on physical processes across all branches of physics. The most important conservation laws include those for energy, linear momentum, angular momentum, and electric charge.

Conservation of energy asserts that the total energy of an isolated system remains constant, although it can transform between various forms such as kinetic, potential, thermal, electrical, chemical, and nuclear. No process can create or destroy energy; it only changes form. This principle is exact and has no known exceptions.

Conservation of linear momentum states that the total vector momentum of an isolated system is constant. If no net external force acts on the system, the vector sum of the momenta of all parts remains unchanged. This leads to the familiar result that internal interactions alone cannot alter the motion of the system's center of mass.

Conservation of angular momentum holds that the total angular momentum of an isolated system remains constant in both magnitude and direction when no external torques act. This explains phenomena such as the stability of planetary orbits and the behavior of rotating systems.

Conservation of electric charge dictates that the net electric charge in any process remains constant. Charge can be transferred or redistributed, but the total amount is unchanged in all known interactions.

These conservation laws are deeply connected to symmetries of the laws of nature through Noether's theorem. This theorem states that every continuous symmetry of the action of a physical system corresponds to a conserved quantity. Time-translation symmetry (the laws of physics are the same at all times) leads to conservation of energy. Spatial-translation symmetry (the laws are the same everywhere in space) yields conservation of linear momentum. Rotational symmetry (the laws are independent of orientation) gives conservation of angular momentum.

Conservation laws are invaluable for solving physical problems because they provide constraints that simplify analysis without requiring detailed knowledge of internal dynamics. They limit possible outcomes of interactions, enable predictions about inaccessible systems, and serve as checks on theoretical models and experimental results across classical mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum mechanics, and particle physics.

#Classical mechanics

#Kinematics

Kinematics is the branch of classical mechanics that describes the motion of points, objects, and systems without reference to the causes of that motion, focusing instead on trajectories and differential properties such as position, velocity, and acceleration.

Motion is always described relative to a chosen reference frame, a coordinate system that defines positions and times. Position specifies an object's location within this frame at a given time. Displacement is the vector change in position, calculated as Δx=x−x0​ in one dimension, where x is the final position and x0​ is the initial position.

Velocity characterizes how position changes over time. Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the elapsed time interval, vˉ=ΔtΔx​. Instantaneous velocity is the instantaneous rate of change of position, defined as the derivative v(t)=dtdx​, or the limit of average velocity as the time interval approaches zero. Speed is the magnitude of velocity.

Acceleration measures the rate of change of velocity. Average acceleration is aˉ=ΔtΔv​=t−t0​v−v0​​, where v0​ and v are initial and final velocities. Instantaneous acceleration is the derivative a(t)=dtdv​.

For motion with constant acceleration, kinematic equations relate position, velocity, acceleration, and time:
v=v0​+at,
x=x0​+v0​t+21​at2,
v2=v02​+2a(x−x0​),
and x=x0​+2(v0​+v)​t,
where v0​ is initial velocity, v is final velocity, a is constant acceleration, x0​ is initial position, x is final position, and t is time.

Projectile motion exemplifies two-dimensional kinematics under constant vertical acceleration due to gravity alone. The motion separates into independent horizontal and vertical components: horizontal velocity remains constant (ax​=0), while vertical acceleration is −g (downward, where g≈9.80m/s2). Initial velocity components are v0x​=v0​cosθ and v0y​=v0​sinθ, with θ the launch angle. The trajectory is parabolic, with range and maximum height derivable from the constant-acceleration equations applied separately to each component.

Relative motion arises when observers use different reference frames. The velocity of an object relative to one frame equals its velocity relative to a second frame plus the velocity of the second frame relative to the first: vP/E​=vP/T​+vT/E​, for example. This vector addition extends to multiple frames and two or three dimensions, explaining how motion appears different from moving observers.

#Dynamics and Newton's laws

Dynamics is the branch of classical mechanics concerned with the effects of forces on the motion of objects, explaining how forces produce changes in velocity or acceleration.

Newton's three laws of motion, formulated by Isaac Newton, form the foundation of classical dynamics.

Newton's first law, also known as the law of inertia, states that an object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues in uniform motion in a straight line, unless acted upon by a net external force. This law establishes that constant velocity (including zero velocity) is the natural state in the absence of unbalanced forces, and inertia measures an object's resistance to changes in motion.

Newton's second law quantifies the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration, stating that the net force acting on an object equals its mass times its acceleration:

Fnet​=ma

where Fnet​ is the vector sum of all forces, m is the object's mass, and a is its acceleration. Acceleration is directly proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass, with both net force and acceleration as vectors sharing the same direction. This law enables prediction of an object's motion given the forces acting on it and applies to everyday phenomena such as vehicles accelerating or decelerating under applied forces.

Newton's third law asserts that for every force one object exerts on a second object, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force on the first. These action-reaction pairs always act on different bodies and are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. This law underlies interactions such as propulsion, where expelling mass backward produces forward motion, and implies conservation of momentum for isolated systems.

To analyze forces and apply Newton's laws—particularly the second law—free-body diagrams are essential tools. A free-body diagram isolates an object and depicts all external forces acting on it as vectors originating from the object's center, with arrow lengths indicating relative magnitudes and directions showing orientations. Forces are labeled by type (e.g., gravity, normal, friction, tension). The net force is found by vector addition of these forces, determining acceleration via the second law.

Common forces in free-body diagrams include:

Gravity (weight), acting downward.

Normal force, perpendicular to a supporting surface.

Tension, along ropes or strings, pulling equally at both ends in ideal cases.

Friction, opposing relative motion or tendency to motion between surfaces.

Applied forces, such as pushes or pulls.

Examples illustrate these concepts. For a book at rest on a table, the free-body diagram shows gravity downward and normal force upward, equal in magnitude, yielding zero net force and no acceleration, consistent with the first law. When pushed horizontally across the table, an applied force acts forward, friction opposes backward, gravity and normal remain vertical; if the applied force exceeds static friction, kinetic friction applies, and net horizontal force produces acceleration per the second law.

For tension, consider a mass suspended from a ceiling by a string: the free-body diagram shows tension upward balancing gravity downward, resulting in equilibrium. In systems involving pulleys or connected objects, tension transmits force along the string, often uniform in magnitude for massless, frictionless strings.

Friction examples include static friction preventing a box from sliding down a ramp until a threshold is reached, or kinetic friction reducing speed of a sliding object. These cases use free-body diagrams to identify component forces parallel and perpendicular to surfaces, resolve them, and compute net force for acceleration.

#Newtonian gravity

Newton's law of universal gravitation describes gravity as an attractive force acting instantaneously between any two masses. The force between two point masses m1​ and m2​ separated by distance r is given by

F=Gr2m1​m2​​,

where G is the gravitational constant, measured as approximately 6.674×10−11m3kg−1s−2. This inverse-square dependence means the force weakens rapidly with increasing distance while remaining directly proportional to the product of the masses.

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass that a test particle would experience there. For a spherical mass M, the field strength g at distance r from its center is

g=Gr2M​,

directed toward the mass. Near Earth's surface, where r approximates Earth's radius, g is nearly constant at about 9.80m/s2. The weight of an object of mass m is then the gravitational force acting on it, w=mg.

Newton applied his law to celestial motion, showing that the gravitational interaction between the Sun and planets produces the centripetal force required for orbital paths. He demonstrated that the inverse-square force law derives Kepler's three empirical laws: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus, the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, and the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its semi-major axis.

Although highly successful for solar system scales and everyday phenomena, Newtonian gravity requires refinement in the framework of general relativity for cases involving very strong fields or high precision.

#Thermodynamics

#Laws of thermodynamics

The laws of thermodynamics are four fundamental principles that govern heat, work, energy transformations, and the direction of physical processes in thermodynamic systems.

The zeroth law establishes the concept of thermal equilibrium and temperature. If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This law justifies the use of thermometers and temperature scales by ensuring that systems in mutual equilibrium share the same temperature.

The first law expresses the conservation of energy in thermodynamic contexts. The change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to the system minus the work done by the system:

ΔU=Q−W

where positive Q denotes heat transferred into the system and positive W denotes work done by the system. Internal energy is a state function dependent only on the system's state, while heat and work are process-dependent quantities.

The second law dictates the direction of natural processes and imposes limits on energy conversion efficiency. Heat cannot spontaneously transfer from a colder body to a hotter body, and no cyclic process can convert heat entirely into work without rejecting some heat to a colder reservoir. These constraints explain the irreversibility of natural processes and the impossibility of a perfectly efficient heat engine.

The third law states that the entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is zero at absolute zero temperature (0 K). This law implies that absolute zero is unattainable in a finite number of steps.

Heat engines operate cyclically between a hot reservoir and a cold reservoir to convert heat into mechanical work. The second law limits their efficiency, with the maximum achievable value given by the Carnot efficiency for a reversible engine:

η=1−TH​TC​​

where TH​ and TC​ are the absolute temperatures (in kelvin) of the hot and cold reservoirs, respectively. This efficiency is the theoretical upper limit; real engines fall below it due to irreversibilities.

Heat transfers via three primary modes. Conduction occurs through matter without bulk motion of the material, such as through a solid wall. Convection involves heat transfer by the bulk motion of a fluid. Radiation transfers energy through electromagnetic waves and requires no intervening medium.

Thermodynamic processes describe changes in system variables. An isobaric process maintains constant pressure. An isochoric process maintains constant volume. An isothermal process maintains constant temperature. An adiabatic process involves no heat transfer. These processes form the basis for analyzing cycles in heat engines and other systems.

#Entropy

Entropy is a thermodynamic state function that quantifies the portion of a system's thermal energy unavailable for conversion into useful work, serving as a measure of disorder or randomness within the system. Introduced by Rudolf Clausius in 1865, entropy arises from the second law of thermodynamics and the Clausius inequality, which states that for any cyclic process, the cyclic integral of δQ/T is less than or equal to zero, with equality holding only for reversible processes. The change in entropy for a reversible process is calculated as ΔS = ∫ (δQ_rev / T), where δQ_rev represents the reversible heat transfer and T is the absolute temperature. For irreversible processes, the entropy change exceeds this integral, reflecting entropy generation due to irreversibilities.

In reversible processes, idealized transformations occur without net entropy production, meaning the total entropy change of the system and its surroundings is zero. This occurs because any entropy decrease in one part is exactly balanced by an increase in another. Irreversible processes, characteristic of all real phenomena, generate positive entropy, with the total entropy change of the system plus surroundings always positive. Entropy generation quantifies the magnitude of irreversibilities, such as heat transfer across finite temperature differences or dissipative effects, and is expressed as S_gen = ΔS_total - ∫ (δQ / T), where S_gen ≥ 0, with equality only for reversible cases. This entropy production leads to lost work, the difference between the work obtainable in a reversible process and that in the actual irreversible one, given by W_lost = T_0 S_gen, where T_0 is the surroundings temperature.

The second law of thermodynamics dictates that the entropy of an isolated system always increases or, in the limiting case of reversible processes, remains constant. This unidirectional increase in entropy establishes the thermodynamic arrow of time, as natural processes proceed toward states of greater disorder, providing a direction from past to future that distinguishes reversible time-symmetric microscopic laws from macroscopic irreversibility. The principle implies that processes occur spontaneously only in the direction of increasing overall entropy or molecular disorder.

The continual increase in the entropy of the universe points toward a future state of maximum entropy, known as the heat death. In this scenario, all energy becomes uniformly dispersed, eliminating temperature gradients and the capacity for spontaneous processes or useful work, resulting in a state of thermal equilibrium where no further changes occur. This ultimate consequence of the second law reflects the inexorable tendency toward energy dispersion in isolated systems.

#Statistical mechanics

Statistical mechanics applies probability theory to large assemblies of particles to derive the macroscopic thermodynamic properties of systems from their microscopic dynamics. It bridges the gap between the deterministic motion of individual particles governed by classical mechanics and the statistical laws of thermodynamics observed in bulk matter.

A central distinction in statistical mechanics is between microstates and macrostates. A microstate fully specifies the position and momentum of every particle in the system, corresponding to a single point in phase space. A macrostate is characterized by macroscopic variables such as total energy, volume, and particle number; each macrostate corresponds to an enormous number of compatible microstates. In isolated systems with fixed energy, the fundamental postulate asserts that all accessible microstates are equally probable.

The entropy $ S $ of a macrostate is defined by Boltzmann's formula:

S=klnΩ

where $ k $ is Boltzmann's constant and $ \Omega $ (or $ W $) is the number of microstates consistent with the macrostate. This expression, introduced by Ludwig Boltzmann, interprets entropy as a measure of the multiplicity or disorder of microscopic configurations. Systems evolve toward equilibrium macrostates with the largest $ \Omega $, explaining the second law of thermodynamics as a statistical tendency toward higher probability rather than an absolute prohibition.

For systems in thermal equilibrium with a large heat reservoir at temperature $ T $, the appropriate description is the canonical ensemble. The probability $ p_i $ that the system occupies a microstate $ i $ with energy $ E_i $ follows the Boltzmann distribution:

pi​=Ze−Ei​/kT​

where the exponential term $ e^{-E_i / kT} $ is the Boltzmann factor, favoring lower-energy states at finite temperatures. The normalization constant $ Z $ is the partition function:

Z=i∑​e−Ei​/kT

In classical statistical mechanics, the sum becomes an integral over phase space:

Z=h3NN!1​∫e−H(q,p)/kTd3Nqd3Np

with $ H $ the classical Hamiltonian, $ N $ the number of particles, and factors accounting for phase-space volume and particle indistinguishability. The partition function contains all thermodynamic information; thermodynamic potentials and averages, such as the Helmholtz free energy $ F = -kT \ln Z $ and mean energy $ \langle E \rangle = -\partial \ln Z / \partial \beta $ (with $ \beta = 1/kT $), derive directly from it.

The statistical framework shows how thermodynamic laws emerge from microscopic probabilities in systems with many particles.

#Electromagnetism

#Electric and magnetic fields

Electric fields arise from electric charges and mediate the electrostatic forces between them. The fundamental law describing the force between two stationary point charges is Coulomb's law, which states that the magnitude of the force is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, with the force being repulsive for like charges and attractive for opposite charges.

The electric field E at a point in space is defined as the electrostatic force F exerted on a small positive test charge q0​ placed at that point, divided by the magnitude of the test charge: E=F/q0​. The direction of the electric field is the direction of the force on a positive test charge. For a point charge q, the electric field is radial, pointing outward from positive charges and inward toward negative charges.

Gauss's law provides a qualitative relationship between electric fields and charge distributions: the net electric flux through any closed surface (the integral of E over the surface, accounting for magnitude and orientation) is proportional to the net electric charge enclosed within that surface. This implies that electric field lines originate on positive charges and terminate on negative charges, with the net flux depending only on the enclosed charge and not on the surface's shape or external charges. This principle is especially useful for symmetric charge distributions.

Magnetic fields originate from moving electric charges or steady electric currents and exert forces on other moving charges or currents. The magnetic force on a charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B is given by the Lorentz force law (magnetic part): F=q(v×B). This force is always perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field, does no work on the charge (changing its direction but not its speed), and is zero if the charge is stationary or moves parallel to the field. The magnitude is F=qvBsinθ, where θ is the angle between v and B. The direction follows the right-hand rule.

#Maxwell's equations

Maxwell's equations are the set of four fundamental equations that unify electricity, magnetism, and light as manifestations of the electromagnetic field. Formulated by James Clerk Maxwell in the 1860s, they describe how electric fields E and magnetic fields B are generated by charges, currents, and time-varying fields.

The equations exist in equivalent integral and differential forms. The integral forms relate field fluxes and circulations to enclosed charges and currents over surfaces and loops, while the differential forms (derived via Gauss's divergence theorem and Stokes' theorem) describe local relationships using divergence and curl operators.

In SI units, the differential forms are:

∇⋅E=ϵ0​ρ​

(Gauss's law for electricity, where ρ is charge density and ϵ0​ is vacuum permittivity)

∇⋅B=0

(Gauss's law for magnetism, implying no magnetic monopoles)

∇×E=−∂t∂B​

(Faraday's law, showing that time-varying magnetic fields induce electric fields)

∇×B=μ0​J+μ0​ϵ0​∂t∂E​

(Ampère-Maxwell law, where J is current density, μ0​ is vacuum permeability, and the term μ0​ϵ0​∂t∂E​ is the displacement current contribution)

The integral forms are:

∮S​E⋅dA=ϵ0​Qenc​​

∮S​B⋅dA=0

∮C​E⋅dl=−dtd​∫S​B⋅dA

[∮C​B⋅dl](/page/Listo​fe​lectromagnetisme​quations)=[μ0​](/page/Vacuump​ermeability)(Ienc​+[ϵ0​dtd​∫S​E⋅dA](/page/Displacementc​urrent))

where Qenc​ is enclosed charge, Ienc​ is enclosed conduction current, and the integrals are over closed surfaces S or loops C.

Maxwell introduced the displacement current term ϵ0​∂t∂E​ to resolve an inconsistency in the original Ampère's law when applied to time-varying fields, such as in charging capacitors where no conduction current flows between plates but a magnetic field is still produced. This term ensures consistency with the continuity equation ∇⋅J=−∂t∂ρ​ and allows changing electric fields to generate magnetic fields.

The inclusion of displacement current leads to the prediction of propagating electromagnetic waves. In vacuum (where ρ=0 and J=0), combining Faraday's law and the Ampère-Maxwell law yields wave equations for E and B with propagation speed c=μ0​ϵ0​​1​, matching the measured speed of light and indicating that light is an electromagnetic wave.

#Electromagnetic radiation

Electromagnetic radiation consists of self-propagating waves of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation. These transverse waves transport energy through space and require no medium, allowing them to travel through vacuum at the speed of light c≈3×108 m/s.

The waves exhibit polarization, determined by the orientation of the electric field vector relative to the direction of propagation. Polarization can be linear, circular, or elliptical, and it affects phenomena such as the reflection of light or the operation of polarizing filters.

The electromagnetic spectrum spans a continuous range of wavelengths or frequencies, from very long radio waves to extremely short gamma rays. The principal regions include radio waves (longest wavelengths, used for broadcasting and astronomy), microwaves (for communication and remote sensing), infrared radiation (associated with thermal emission), visible light (the narrow band perceptible to human vision), ultraviolet radiation (from solar sources), X-rays (high-energy, penetrating radiation), and gamma rays (highest energy, produced in nuclear processes and astrophysical events).

The directional energy flux of an electromagnetic wave is given by the Poynting vector S=μ0​1​E×B, where E is the electric field, B is the magnetic field, and μ0​ is the permeability of free space. The vector points in the direction of wave propagation, and its magnitude represents the instantaneous power per unit area. For a monochromatic plane wave, the time-averaged Poynting vector magnitude is ⟨S⟩=21​cϵ0​E02​, corresponding to the wave's intensity.

Electromagnetic radiation arises fundamentally from accelerating electric charges. In the nonrelativistic limit, the power radiated by an accelerating point charge is given by the Larmor formula P=6πcμ0​q2a2​, where q is the charge, a is the magnitude of acceleration, and c is the speed of light. This power scales with the square of the acceleration, and the radiation pattern is dipolar, with intensity proportional to sin2θ (maximum perpendicular to the acceleration direction and zero along it).

#Relativity

#Special relativity

Special relativity is a fundamental theory in physics, formulated by Albert Einstein in 1905, that describes the relationship between space, time, and the motion of objects at constant velocities, particularly near the speed of light, while reconciling Newtonian mechanics with electromagnetism.

The theory rests on two postulates. First, the laws of physics take the same form in all inertial reference frames (systems moving at constant velocity relative to one another). Second, the speed of light in vacuum, denoted c (approximately 3×108 m/s), is constant and independent of the motion of the source or the observer.

These postulates lead to the Lorentz transformations, which replace the classical Galilean transformations for relating space and time coordinates between inertial frames. For two frames where one moves at constant velocity v along the x-axis relative to the other, the transformations are:

x′=γ(x−vt),t′=γ(t−c2vx​),y′=y,z′=z

where the Lorentz factor is γ=1−c2v2​​1​.

Key consequences include time dilation and length contraction. Time dilation means that a clock moving at speed v relative to an observer runs slower as measured by that observer; the proper time interval Δτ (measured in the clock's rest frame) relates to the time Δt in the observer's frame by Δτ=Δt/γ. Length contraction means that an object's length, measured parallel to its direction of motion, appears shorter in a frame where it moves; the length L observed is L=L0​/γ, where L0​ is the proper length in the object's rest frame (lengths perpendicular to motion are unchanged).

Special relativity also yields mass-energy equivalence. The total relativistic energy of a particle with rest mass m moving at speed v is E=γmc2. At rest (v=0, so γ=1), this reduces to the rest energy E=mc2, showing that mass is a form of energy. The relativistic kinetic energy is then (γ−1)mc2. This equivalence, derived from applying the postulates to energy and momentum conservation, implies that mass can be converted into energy and vice versa, with profound implications for processes like nuclear reactions.

Special relativity applies to inertial motion in flat spacetime; its extension to noninertial motion and gravitation appears in general relativity.

#General relativity

General relativity is Albert Einstein's geometric theory of gravitation, which describes gravity as the curvature of four-dimensional spacetime caused by the presence of mass and energy, rather than as a traditional force acting at a distance. In this framework, mass-energy warps the geometry of spacetime, and objects respond by following the paths dictated by that geometry. The theory extends special relativity to include gravity and has been confirmed by numerous observations, fundamentally replacing Newton's instantaneous action-at-a-distance with a dynamic, geometric description of gravitational phenomena.

The foundation of general relativity rests on the equivalence principle, particularly in its Einsteinian form, which states that the local effects of a uniform gravitational field are indistinguishable from those experienced in a uniformly accelerating reference frame. For example, an observer in a freely falling elevator cannot perform any local experiment to distinguish whether they are in free fall under gravity or floating in empty space far from any masses; all physical laws, including those of special relativity, hold identically in such locally inertial frames. This principle extends to the weak form (equality of inertial and gravitational mass, leading to universal free fall) and the strong form (all laws of physics, including gravitational self-energy, behave the same in freely falling frames). The equivalence principle implies that gravity is not a force but a manifestation of spacetime geometry.

In curved spacetime, free particles and light follow geodesics, which are the analogs of straight lines in flat space—the shortest or extremal paths through the geometry. These paths are determined by the spacetime metric, which encodes the curvature, and satisfy the geodesic equation that arises from extremizing proper time along the worldline. Massive particles trace timelike geodesics, while light follows null geodesics; deviations from straight-line motion in flat space, such as planetary orbits or light deflection, emerge naturally as motion along these curved geodesics.

The Einstein field equations relate the curvature of spacetime, described by the Einstein tensor, to the distribution of matter and energy, captured by the stress-energy tensor. Conceptually, they express that matter and energy tell spacetime how to curve, while the resulting curved spacetime tells matter and energy how to move; this mutual interaction forms a nonlinear system governing gravitational phenomena across scales. In the weak-field limit, the equations reduce to Newton's law of universal gravitation.

General relativity predicts several observable effects that distinguish it from Newtonian gravity. Light rays bend in the presence of massive bodies, as famously confirmed during the 1919 solar eclipse when starlight grazing the Sun was deflected by approximately 1.75 arcseconds, matching the theory's prediction. Extreme curvature leads to black holes, regions where spacetime is so warped that no light or matter can escape beyond the event horizon. Accelerating massive objects, such as merging black holes, produce ripples in spacetime known as gravitational waves that propagate at the speed of light; these were directly detected in 2015 by the LIGO observatory from a binary black hole merger, confirming a century-old prediction and opening a new window for observing the universe.

#Quantum mechanics

#Wave-particle duality

Wave-particle duality describes the fundamental quantum phenomenon in which entities such as light and matter display both particle-like and wave-like properties, depending on the experimental context.

The wave nature of light was established through classical experiments demonstrating interference and diffraction. In Thomas Young's double-slit experiment, light passing through two closely spaced slits produces alternating bright and dark fringes on a screen, resulting from the constructive and destructive interference of waves emanating from each slit.

However, the photoelectric effect revealed light's particle-like behavior. When light strikes a metal surface, electrons are ejected only if the light's frequency exceeds a material-specific threshold, independent of intensity. Moreover, the kinetic energy of ejected electrons increases linearly with frequency above the threshold, while intensity affects only the number of ejected electrons. Classical wave theory failed to explain these frequency-dependent effects, as it predicted emission based solely on accumulated energy from wave intensity. In 1905, Albert Einstein resolved this by proposing that light consists of discrete quanta—now called photons—each carrying energy proportional to its frequency, leading to instantaneous energy transfer in particle-like collisions with electrons.

This duality extends to matter. Motivated by the established dual nature of light, Louis de Broglie hypothesized in 1924 that particles such as electrons also possess associated waves, with the wavelength inversely related to the particle's momentum. This proposed that matter could exhibit interference and diffraction phenomena.

The hypothesis was experimentally verified by the Davisson-Germer experiment in 1927. Electrons accelerated toward a nickel crystal target scattered with intensity peaks at specific angles, forming diffraction patterns analogous to those observed with X-rays diffracting from crystal lattices. These patterns matched predictions based on de Broglie's wavelength and Bragg's law of diffraction, confirming that electrons behave as waves under these conditions.

Electron diffraction and the double-slit experiment performed with electrons further demonstrate this duality: individual electrons arrive at discrete points on a detector, yet over time they build up an interference pattern characteristic of waves, even when emitted one at a time. These results underscore that quantum objects cannot be exclusively classified as particles or waves but exhibit both aspects depending on the measurement.

#Uncertainty principle

The uncertainty principle, also known as the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, is a fundamental limit in quantum mechanics stating that certain pairs of physical properties of a particle cannot be measured or known simultaneously with arbitrary precision. The most famous form relates position and momentum:

ΔxΔp≥2ℏ​

where Δx is the uncertainty (standard deviation) in position, Δp is the uncertainty in momentum, and ℏ=h/2π is the reduced Planck constant. This inequality, first derived rigorously by Earle Hesse Kennard in 1927 and generalized by Howard Robertson in 1929, follows from the non-commutativity of the position and momentum operators ([x,p]=iℏ) in quantum mechanics.

Werner Heisenberg originally proposed the principle in 1927 through thought experiments, such as observing an electron with a gamma-ray microscope. To determine position precisely requires short-wavelength (high-energy) photons, which, via the Compton effect, impart a significant and uncontrollable momentum kick to the electron, increasing momentum uncertainty. Conversely, longer-wavelength light reduces momentum disturbance but blurs position. Heisenberg thus concluded that simultaneous exact knowledge of position and momentum is impossible; the more accurately one property is known, the less accurately the conjugate property can be known.

A related form concerns energy and time:

ΔEΔt≥2ℏ​

Unlike position and momentum, time is not an observable operator in standard quantum mechanics, so this relation is interpreted differently. It typically describes the trade-off between the uncertainty in a system's energy and the time interval over which that energy can be measured or the lifetime of a quantum state. For example, a short-lived excited atomic state (small Δt) has a correspondingly large energy uncertainty (ΔE), producing broader spectral lines, while a long-lived state has a sharper energy and narrower line. This form is often illustrated in atomic transitions or particle decays.

The physical meaning of the uncertainty principle is not merely a limitation of measurement apparatus but a consequence of the wave-particle duality of matter. A particle with precisely defined momentum has a plane-wave state with uniform probability distribution (infinite position uncertainty), while a localized particle (small Δx) requires a superposition of many wavelengths (large Δp). For macroscopic objects, the uncertainty is negligible due to the smallness of ℏ; for quantum particles such as electrons, it is significant. A classic comparison: an electron with velocity uncertainty Δu=10−3 m/s has Δx≈5.8 cm, while a 6 kg bowling ball with the same Δu has Δx≈10−32 m, far below any detectable scale.

The principle has profound implications for determinism. In classical physics, exact knowledge of position and momentum would allow perfect prediction of future motion via Newton's laws. Quantum mechanics forbids this simultaneous precision, implying that the future state of a system is not fully determined by its present state in the classical sense. Instead, quantum mechanics yields only probabilistic predictions, fundamentally altering the deterministic worldview of classical physics. Heisenberg himself viewed this as showing that the classical "path" of a particle emerges only through observation.

#Schrödinger equation and quantum states

The Schrödinger equation is the fundamental equation of non-relativistic quantum mechanics, describing the time evolution of quantum states.

The time-dependent Schrödinger equation governs the wave function ψ(r,t) of a system:

iℏ∂t∂ψ(r,t)​=H^ψ(r,t)

where H^ is the Hamiltonian operator, typically H^=−2mℏ2​∇2+V(r), with m the particle mass, V(r) the potential, and ℏ the reduced Planck constant.

The wave function ψ(r,t) is complex-valued and normalized such that ∫∣ψ(r,t)∣2dV=1. According to the probability interpretation, ∣ψ(r,t)∣2dV is the probability of finding the particle in volume element dV at position r and time t.

For time-independent Hamiltonians, stationary solutions take the form ψ(r,t)=ϕ(r)e−iEt/ℏ, reducing to the time-independent Schrödinger equation

H^ϕ(r)=Eϕ(r)

where E is the energy eigenvalue and ϕ(r) is the energy eigenfunction. For such eigenstates, the probability density ∣ϕ(r)∣2 is time-independent.

General quantum states are linear superpositions of energy eigenstates:

ψ(r,t)=k∑​ck​ϕk​(r)e−iEk​t/ℏ

with complex coefficients ck​ satisfying normalization ∑k​∣ck​∣2=1. This superposition principle underlies quantum interference and the coherent evolution of states.

The hydrogen atom provides a key exactly solvable case of the time-independent equation with Coulomb potential V(r)=−e2/(4πϵ0​r). Solutions yield quantized energy levels depending only on the principal quantum number n=1,2,3,…:

En​=−n213.6eV​

The full wave functions are ψnlml​​(r,θ,ϕ)=Rnl​(r)Ylml​​(θ,ϕ), where Rnl​(r) is the radial part, Ylml​​ are spherical harmonics, l=0,1,…,n−1 is the azimuthal quantum number (determining orbital angular momentum), and ml​=−l,…,+l is the magnetic quantum number (determining orientation). The probability density ∣ψnlml​​∣2 reveals electron distribution, with radial probability peaking at characteristic distances dependent on n.

Wave-particle duality and the uncertainty principle arise as consequences of the wave function and the Schrödinger equation governing quantum states.

#Branches of physics

#Particle physics

Particle physics is the branch of physics devoted to the study of fundamental particles—the smallest known constituents of matter—and the interactions between them.

The Standard Model provides the theoretical framework for particle physics, describing three of the four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong, and weak) and the particles involved in these interactions, while excluding gravity. Developed in the early 1970s, it has been extensively tested and confirmed by experiments, accurately predicting phenomena and particle properties.

The Standard Model organizes fundamental particles into fermions (matter particles) and bosons (force carriers and the Higgs boson). Fermions are divided into two groups: quarks and leptons, each containing six types ("flavors") arranged in three generations of increasing mass. The first generation includes the most stable particles that form ordinary matter, while heavier generations decay into lighter ones.

Quarks carry fractional electric charge and a property called "color," and they combine to form composite particles such as protons and neutrons. The six quarks are: up and down (first generation), charm and strange (second), and top and bottom (third). Leptons include the electron, muon, and tau (charged) along with their corresponding neutrinos (neutral and nearly massless): electron neutrino, muon neutrino, and tau neutrino. The electron, as a first-generation lepton, is a familiar component of atoms.

Bosons mediate the fundamental forces. The photon carries the electromagnetic force, acting on charged particles over infinite range. Eight gluons mediate the strong force, binding quarks within hadrons over very short distances. The W (charged) and Z (neutral) bosons mediate the weak force, responsible for processes such as beta decay and operating over short ranges. The Higgs boson, discovered in 2012, is associated with the mechanism that gives mass to other particles through their interactions with the Higgs field.

Particle accelerators are essential tools in particle physics, accelerating charged particles such as protons or ions to near the speed of light and colliding them to recreate high-energy conditions. These collisions convert kinetic energy into new particles for study, probing the Standard Model and searching for new physics. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, the world's most powerful accelerator, collides protons at energies up to 13.6 TeV in a 27-kilometer ring, enabling discoveries including the Higgs boson and detailed measurements of particle properties.

The Standard Model is formulated within quantum field theory, providing the mathematical basis for describing these particle interactions and forces.

#Condensed matter physics

Condensed matter physics is the branch of physics that studies the macroscopic properties of solids, liquids, and other condensed phases of matter, using the laws of microscopic quantum mechanics to explain the collective behavior of large numbers of atoms, electrons, or molecules. This field addresses emergent phenomena arising from interactions in these systems, underpinning much of modern technology through materials like semiconductors and superconductors.

In crystalline solids, atoms arrange in highly ordered, periodic lattices, such as face-centered cubic or body-centered cubic structures, which determine key physical properties including density, bonding strength, and mechanical characteristics. The periodic arrangement influences how atoms bond, often through ionic or covalent mechanisms, and affects the overall material behavior.

Band theory explains the electronic structure of crystalline solids, where the discrete energy levels of isolated atoms broaden into nearly continuous energy bands due to the periodic lattice potential and quantum mechanical overlap of wave functions. The valence band is the highest occupied band at absolute zero, while the conduction band lies above it, separated by an energy gap. In metals, the valence band is partially filled, allowing electrons to respond to electric fields and conduct electricity readily; insulators have a large energy gap that prevents conduction; semiconductors possess a smaller gap (typically around 1 eV), enabling limited thermal excitation of electrons from the valence to conduction band and tunable conductivity.

Semiconductors, with electrical conductivity intermediate between conductors and insulators, have their properties precisely controlled through doping, introducing impurities to create n-type materials (with excess electrons) or p-type materials (with excess holes). Combining these forms p-n junctions, where a depletion region arises from carrier diffusion, establishing an internal electric field. Forward bias narrows the depletion region and allows exponential current increase, while reverse bias widens it and blocks current, enabling diodes to act as one-way valves. Junction transistors, typically n-p-n structures, use a small base current to control a much larger collector current, providing amplification and switching essential for electronic circuits and integrated devices.

Superconductivity occurs in certain materials below a critical temperature, where electrical resistance drops to zero and magnetic fields are expelled from the material interior (Meissner effect). This is attributed to electrons forming Cooper pairs that move coherently without scattering.

Superfluidity is a related macroscopic quantum phenomenon, observed in liquid helium-4 below approximately 2.17 K, where the liquid flows without viscosity through narrow channels, arising from Bose-Einstein condensation of bosonic atoms. Superconductivity and superfluidity represent universal emergent quantum states in fermionic and bosonic systems, respectively.

Phase transitions in condensed matter involve abrupt or continuous changes in material order, such as from normal to superconducting or liquid to superfluid states, often linked to symmetry breaking and entropy changes reflected in configurational differences between phases. These transitions are central to understanding collective behavior in condensed systems.

#Astrophysics and cosmology

Astrophysics and cosmology apply the laws of physics to celestial bodies, galaxies, and the universe as a whole, bridging microscopic physical processes with macroscopic phenomena on cosmic scales. Astrophysics examines the formation, structure, and evolution of stars and other astronomical objects, while cosmology investigates the origin, composition, structure, and fate of the universe.

Stellar structure and evolution describe how stars form from dense interstellar clouds of gas and dust, collapsing under gravity to become protostars surrounded by accretion disks and often ejecting jets of material. These young stellar objects contract and heat up during the pre-main-sequence phase, with low-mass stars showing variability and high-mass stars limited by strong radiation. Once hydrogen fusion ignites in the core, stars enter the main sequence, where fusion of hydrogen into helium powers them, with lifetimes determined primarily by initial mass: massive stars exhaust fuel rapidly in millions of years, while low-mass red dwarfs persist for trillions of years, far exceeding the current age of the universe.

After exhausting core hydrogen, moderate-mass stars like the Sun expand into red giants, fusing helium into carbon and oxygen in their cores before shedding outer layers to leave white dwarfs. High-mass stars fuse progressively heavier elements up to iron, then undergo core collapse and supernova explosions, which may leave neutron stars or black holes and enrich the interstellar medium with heavy elements that seed future star formation. Pulsating stars such as Cepheids, driven by internal instabilities, serve as distance indicators, while asteroseismology uses surface vibrations to probe stellar interiors.

Cosmology describes the universe's origin and evolution starting with the Big Bang approximately 13.8 billion years ago, when the universe expanded from a hot, dense state. A brief period of cosmic inflation immediately followed, rapidly expanding the universe and smoothing out initial quantum fluctuations to produce the observed large-scale uniformity. Within minutes, Big Bang nucleosynthesis produced the light elements hydrogen, helium, and traces of lithium, accounting for their observed cosmic abundances.

About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe cooled sufficiently for electrons to combine with protons to form neutral atoms in the epoch of recombination, making the universe transparent and releasing photons that form the cosmic microwave background (CMB). This relic radiation, now cooled to a uniform temperature of about 2.725 K with tiny anisotropies of order one part in 100,000, provides a snapshot of the early universe and reveals density fluctuations that seeded galaxy formation. The CMB's uniformity across the sky, despite regions never having been in causal contact, supports cosmic inflation, while its polarization patterns offer further insights into primordial processes.

The universe's mass-energy content consists of approximately 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter, and 68% dark energy. Dark matter, invisible and undetected directly, exerts gravitational influence that organizes galaxies and clusters, evidenced by flat galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing in clusters like the Bullet Cluster, and CMB fluctuations. Dark energy drives the observed accelerated expansion of the universe, discovered through type Ia supernova observations in 1998 and confirmed by CMB measurements and baryon acoustic oscillations in large-scale galaxy distributions. Applications of general relativity underpin cosmological models describing this expansion and phenomena such as gravitational lensing.

#Nuclear physics

Nuclear physics is the branch of physics that studies atomic nuclei—the dense cores of atoms composed of protons and neutrons (collectively called nucleons)—along with their structure, stability, reactions, and the forces binding them.

The primary force holding the nucleus together is the residual strong nuclear force, an attractive interaction between nucleons that operates over short ranges (on the order of a few femtometers) and overcomes the electromagnetic repulsion among positively charged protons.

Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons, arising from the mass defect—the difference between the mass of the separated nucleons and the actual nuclear mass—converted to energy via Einstein's relation $ E = \Delta m , c^2 $.

The binding energy per nucleon, obtained by dividing the total binding energy by the mass number $ A $, varies with $ A $ and forms a curve that peaks near iron-56 (approximately 8.8 MeV per nucleon) and nickel-62 (the most tightly bound nuclide), indicating maximum stability for medium-mass nuclei.

This binding energy curve explains energy release in nuclear reactions: fusion combines light nuclei (such as deuterium and tritium) to form heavier ones closer to the peak, while fission splits heavy nuclei (such as uranium-235) into medium-mass fragments nearer the peak; both processes convert mass to energy as the products are more tightly bound.

Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei toward more stable states, primarily through three types: alpha decay (emission of a helium-4 nucleus, reducing $ A $ by 4 and atomic number $ Z $ by 2), beta decay (conversion of a neutron to a proton or vice versa, accompanied by an electron or positron and an antineutrino or neutrino), and gamma decay (emission of high-energy photons from excited nuclear states to lower energy levels).

Nuclear fission involves a heavy nucleus splitting into two or more lighter fragments, often releasing additional neutrons and large amounts of energy; nuclear fusion combines light nuclei into heavier ones, releasing energy and powering stellar processes such as hydrogen-to-helium conversion in stars.

Nuclear models describe nuclear properties and stability. The liquid drop model treats the nucleus as an incompressible fluid drop, accounting for binding energy via the semi-empirical mass formula with terms for volume (cohesive nucleon attraction), surface (reduced binding at the nuclear boundary), Coulomb (proton repulsion), symmetry (preference for equal proton-neutron numbers), and pairing (enhanced stability in even-even nuclei).

The shell model views nucleons as occupying discrete quantum energy levels analogous to atomic electron shells, explaining enhanced stability at "magic numbers" of protons or neutrons (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) due to filled shells and incorporating spin-orbit coupling for level splitting.

Nuclear states are governed by quantum mechanics.

#Other branches

Other branches of physics include several specialized and interdisciplinary fields that apply fundamental principles to specific phenomena.

Acoustics is the branch of physics concerned with the production, control, transmission, reception, and effects of sound. It deals with mechanical waves in media such as gases, liquids, and solids, encompassing subfields like physical acoustics (wave-matter interactions), architectural acoustics (room sound design), musical acoustics, environmental acoustics, and ultrasonics (high-frequency waves). Acoustics supports applications in audio engineering, medical imaging (ultrasound), noise control, and underwater communication.

Optics is one of the oldest branches of physics, devoted to the study of light, its propagation, interaction with matter, and related phenomena. Beyond basic electromagnetic theory, it includes geometrical optics (ray tracing for lenses and mirrors), physical optics (wave phenomena like diffraction, interference, and polarization), and aspects of quantum optics. Optics underpins technologies such as lasers, fiber optics, imaging systems, and spectroscopy.

Plasma physics examines plasma, the fourth state of matter, consisting of ionized gas with free electrons and ions that exhibit collective behavior under electromagnetic forces. Plasmas dominate the visible universe (stars, nebulae, interstellar medium) and are central to magnetic confinement fusion research for clean energy, as well as applications in semiconductor manufacturing, space propulsion, and environmental technologies.

Biophysics applies theories, methods, and quantitative tools from physics to understand biological systems across scales—from molecules and cells to organisms and ecosystems. It bridges physics and biology, enabling advances in structural biology (protein folding, DNA structure), cellular dynamics, neuroscience modeling, medical imaging (MRI, PET), biomaterials, and environmental processes.

Geophysics applies physics principles to investigate Earth's structure, dynamics, and environment through physical measurements. It encompasses seismology (earthquake waves), geomagnetism, gravity studies, and geodynamics, providing insights into plate tectonics, Earth's interior composition, natural hazards, and climate-related processes. These fields often intersect with core physics theories while addressing domain-specific questions.
